name: Tax Justice Network (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result at the defaults by income group: revenue in low and lower-middle income countries other than India 78% (equally over the nine African countries whose tax authorities the network works with in its 2025 report, Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, Uganda, Ethiopia, Zambia, Tanzania, Rwanda and Benin, and Pakistan, Bangladesh and the Philippines), India 9% (valued at GiveWell's lower figure for its government), upper-middle income 10% (Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, South Africa), high income 3% (the UK as a stand-in). A judgment: no country split of the revenue or losses is published.
summary: The Tax Justice Network, a UK non-profit research and advocacy company founded in 2003 (GBP 2.09 million spent in 2025), proposed the tax-transparency standards now in force worldwide (automatic exchange of tax information, ownership registers, country-by-country reporting) and campaigns for the UN tax convention due in 2027. An average year of its spending since 2003 (from its accounts, about 45% of 2025's in real terms) is counted against its judged 2% share of five years of the revenue those standards raise (the OECD Global Forum's EUR 4 billion a year, 70% in developing countries), and against 6% of a 40% chance that the convention recovers a twentieth of the US$47 billion lower-income countries lose each year, two thirds of that work already done. Revenue in low and lower-middle income countries is valued as GiveWell values government spending there (about 1.5 times cash, India's a quarter of that), elsewhere as money spread over citizens' consumption, both net of what the tax costs the rich who pay it. With the next dollar at {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} of the average, it comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars: the work is valued through public revenue for lower-income governments, a large sum of which a small credited share still outweighs a budget under US$3 million a year. The result is mostly uncertainty: the network's share of the credit, the years a win counts and the share of losses the convention recovers are judgments with no study behind them, and its own ranges span over ten-thousandfold; both branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: An average year of what the Tax Justice Network spent since 2003, built from its published accounts for 2005-2025 (hosted bodies left out) in 2025 prices, with judged earlier years, against 2025's audited GBP 2.09 million; fundraising spread over the programme. The network is a UK non-profit company limited by guarantee, not a registered charity; donations from the US are accepted as from an equivalent of a 501(c)(3) public charity.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: The public revenue the two outcomes concern: what the international transparency standards the network proposed in 2003 raise each year (the OECD Global Forum's count, split by income group), and what countries lose each year to cross-border tax abuse, the UN tax convention's target.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What a dollar of public revenue is worth: in low and lower-middle income countries GiveWell's value of a dollar of government spending, elsewhere the money spread over citizens' consumption; both less what the tax costs those who pay it. The standards count the years a won reform counts; the convention is a chance, after a wait.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch's share of the credit (the network's share of the movement's resources, times civil society's share among those who campaigned for it), trust in the figures, the share collected or applied, missing data and side effects; the canonical rows are their outcome-weighted averages, for reading only.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: Both branches' credited value, spread over the 23 years of work since 2003, per dollar of an average year's spending.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Share of the tax at stake that multinationals' profit shifting avoids (the rest: wealthy individuals' offshore wealth)

source.title: Tax Justice Network, The State of Tax Justice 2024
source.quote: two-thirds (US$347.6 billion) is lost to multinational corporations shifting profit offshore

rows.explainer: Of the $492 billion a year lost to cross-border tax abuse, two thirds ($347.6 billion) is multinationals' profit shifting and a third ($144.8 billion) wealthy individuals' offshore wealth (State of Tax Justice 2024): the UN convention's branch. The transparency standards' revenue comes mostly from individuals' offshore accounts (exchange of information, voluntary disclosure). The two branches count about equally here: 50%, range 30% to 70%.

rows.label: Consumption per person of the owners of offshore wealth, as a multiple of the UK average
rows.explainer: Offshore wealth belongs to the very richest: Alstadsaeter, Johannesen and Zucman (2019) find the top 0.01% own about half of the offshore wealth in Scandinavian leaks. Their consumption is far less concentrated than their wealth: judged 20 times UK household consumption per person (8 to 60).

rows.label: Consumption per person of those who pay the tax, as a multiple of the UK average
rows.explainer: A dollar taken from someone consuming c costs 1/c, so the payers' multiple is the dollar-weighted harmonic mean: profit shifting's at the shared figure for those who bear corporate income tax (@public_funds.corporate_tax_payer_multiple, 2.5: three quarters on shareholders, a quarter on workers), offshore wealth's at its owners'. About 4.4.

rows.label: Cost to the payers of a dollar of tax, units of value
rows.explainer: Domestic money's rule (docs/normalization.md 2.20): the recipients' gain less the payers' cost; a dollar taken from someone consuming c costs 1/c in ln(consumption), valued at the shared rate, times the shared marginal cost of public funds (@public_funds.mcpf: the excess burden of tax, including less investment).

rows.label: Value of a dollar of revenue in an upper-middle income country, net of its payers' cost, units of value

rows.label: Consumption per person in the high-income countries that raise the revenue, as a multiple of the UK's
rows.explainer: The high-income revenue is mostly European (France, Germany, Spain, Italy and the UK report the largest sums), with the US and others; judged at UK household consumption per person (0.7 to 1.6 times: southern Europe lower, the US higher).

rows.label: Value of a dollar of revenue in a high-income country, net of its payers' cost, units of value
rows.explainer: The domestic rule again (normalization.md 2.20): spread over citizens' consumption, less the payers' cost. About a hundredth of cash per dollar.

rows.label: Upper-middle income countries' share of the losses outside lower-income countries
rows.explainer: Most profit shifting and offshore wealth costs the US, Europe and Japan; China, Brazil, Mexico and the other upper-middle income countries lose a smaller part. Judged 25% (10% to 40%).

rows.label: Transparency standards: chance the win happened
rows.explainer: The standards are in force: automatic exchange under the Common Reporting Standard since 2017 (over 100 jurisdictions), beneficial-ownership requirements in the FATF and Global Forum standards, country-by-country reporting to tax authorities under BEPS Action 13 since 2016. The network's share of the credit is a_attribution_share_shared.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts

rows.label: UN convention: share of countries' yearly losses its rules would recover if applied in full
rows.explainer: The framework convention's terms cover fair allocation of taxing rights, taxing high-net-worth individuals, illicit financial flows and dispute resolution, through a framework text and early protocols (taxation of cross-border services; disputes). Its own text is due in 2027, the protocols' content and the countries that ratify them uncertain; the nearest reference, the OECD's estimate that its global minimum tax would raise US$155-192 billion a year (about a third of the network's US$480 billion of losses), is an upper anchor for a reform of far wider reach, cut back since by the 2025 exemption of US multinationals; the convention's first protocols (cross-border services, disputes) are narrower. Judged 5% of the losses (1% to 30%), if it comes into force with substance and is applied in full; slow application is in b_implementation_adj only.

source.quote: With the text scheduled for General Assembly agreement in 2027, and the creation of a globally inclusive framework body to follow

rows.explainer: For: the General Assembly votes by majority, every country but the US is negotiating and adoption is scheduled for 2027. Against: OECD members' reluctance, the corporate lobby the network itself names, the US, the one country not negotiating (2025 report p. 4), and the ratifications protocols with substance need. Judged even (0.4 to 1.6 times).

rows.label: Transparency standards: civil society's share among those who campaigned for them
rows.explainer: Among those who pressed for the standards: civil society proposed the measures first and kept them on the agenda; the governments that pushed for them on their own account (the G20's 2009 push after the financial crisis, the US FATCA law of 2010, which made automatic exchange workable, the EU's directives) and the journalists who published the leaks (LuxLeaks, the Panama Papers) did more. The OECD secretariat, the Global Forum's peer reviews and the governments that apply and enforce the standards are the adopters: their part is under the mobiliser's share, not in this one (docs/normalization.md 2.24); that the standards would have come some day is the years a win counts. Judged 35% (20% to 60%).
